summary:
Berlin is a Land of the Federal Republic of Germany and stands under the national framework; legal gender recognition, identity documents, entry and border screening are governed nationally and are covered by the parent record. What is specific to Berlin is the city's own prison administration, its documented record of anti-LGBTIQ+ violence, and the security environment around its Pride events.

The Berlin prison service publishes an information page for trans, inter and non-binary people held in custody. It states that legislation has created a basis for considering their situation, that Berlin prison staff are responsible for taking each detainee's individual needs into account within the legal framework, and it sets out gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling and support offers across the city's facilities, including JVA Moabit and JVA für Frauen Berlin.

MANEO, Berlin's anti-violence documentation project, recorded 723 LSBTIQ+-hostile incidents in the city in 2025, slightly fewer than the 738 documented in 2024, drawn from 1,014 new reports, a new high for incoming reports. Its 12 May 2026 release lists insults, threats and physical attacks on public transport, in parks and in streets, with Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten the most affected districts, plus 58 attacks on LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events. MANEO states that the figures capture only part of reality because of a high dark figure, and reports that its own counselling centre was attacked several times in 2025.

Violence reached the Pride march itself. At the 48th Berlin Christopher Street Day, a vehicle drove into a crowd in the Tiergarten area, killing one woman, injuring several people and forcing the event to be cancelled.

Organisers of Berlin CSD have urged vigilance ahead of the city's Pride, at which hundreds of thousands are expected. Maneo, the Berlin anti-violence documentation project, states that big-city parades such as Berlin and Cologne were not specifically threatened and that smaller towns are hardest to police. A queer café owner in Berlin-Neukölln reports filing 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months.
tangentialFactors:
MANEO's figures are raw counts of incidents reported to one Berlin documentation project, not a per-capita rate, and the project itself states that a high dark figure means the counts capture only part of reality. The 2025 total of 723 sits below the 738 of 2024, so the year-on-year direction is slightly downward even as incoming reports reached a new high of 1,014; neither figure supports a claim that Berlin became safer or more dangerous on its own.

Venue access in Berlin is shaped by house rules rather than law. FLINTA spaces are defined as spaces for women, lesbians, intersex, non-binary, trans and agender people, that is, people who do not fit a cis male gender identity, and were created out of discomfort around cis men and the male domination of many queer spaces. Two long-standing male-exclusive venues, Lab.Oratory and Boiler, historically admitted only male patrons, with cases of feminine men and gender-queer individuals refused entry; their entry policy has evolved since the 2000s to admit more kinds of non-female gender expression, though instances of exclusion still occur, alongside a developing concept of queer masculinities covering gay, bi, trans and queer men.

Contemporary Berlin is described as having a rise in queer spaces catering to marginalised groups within the LGBTQ community, including transgender individuals, which cuts against the venue-exclusion pattern above.
localsOnly:
MANEO runs a counselling centre for people affected by LSBTIQ+ hostility in Berlin and offers victim counselling and an anonymous reporting line on 030-2163336, staffed daily from 17:00 to 19:00. The centre itself was attacked several times in 2025, and the project's own reporting notes that a high dark figure means most incidents never reach its counts.

Residents carry the practical burden of the district pattern: Schöneberg, Neukölln, Kreuzberg, Friedrichshain and Tiergarten are named as the most affected areas, and 58 attacks were recorded against LSBTIQ+ venues, memorials and events during 2025. A queer café owner in Berlin-Neukölln filed 45 police complaints over homophobic attacks in 18 months, a local measure of how often complaints are actually made rather than how often incidents occur.

For people held in the city's prisons, the Berlin prison service page is the resident-facing route to the rules on gender-segregated placement, intake procedures and counselling contacts at facilities including JVA Moabit and JVA für Frauen Berlin.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Berlin-specific case outcome on the placement of a trans detainee is sourced here. The prison service page states principles, responsibilities and procedures; whether Berlin's practice diverges from the national pattern of exceptional-case placement is unresolved in this inventory.

The inventory contains no Berlin-specific rules on identity documents, gender markers, entry or visa screening, and no Berlin-specific provision on legal gender recognition, marriage recognition or conversion therapy; those layers are national and are not restated here.

The counts of attacks on Pride events nationally, and the funding figures for the support fund focused on eastern Germany, come from a national monitoring source and are not carried into this regional entry; no per-parade or per-population denominator is supplied for them.

Whether the 45 police complaints filed by the Neukölln café owner resulted in charges or convictions is not sourced. Historical material on Section 175, the 1933 destruction of the Institute for Sexual Science and post-war decriminalisation is documented in the inventory but does not bear on present-day visitor exposure and is not carried forward.
